# FRC Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v3 (board-approved 17 Sep 2026)

## 1. Core frame
The most powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic harm, and leading AI scientists have warned that the risk extends to human extinction (CAIS Statement on AI Risk, May 2023). These systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. Congress should set binding, enforceable safety requirements, and must not wipe out the state laws that are the only binding rules on the books.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: OPPOSE. A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling. No freeze of SB 53 / RAISE.
- Frontier developers: SUPPORT incident reporting with 72-hour reporting (match RAISE); add mandatory independent third-party audits, published safety frameworks with enforcement, and whistleblower protections at least as strong as SB 53.
- Licensing: ask for a federal licence requirement for training runs above a compute threshold.
- CAISI: SUPPORT codification; ask for mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models and funding well above $100M/yr.

## 3. Language
- Use: "binding, not voluntary", "a floor, not a ceiling", "verify before deploy", "catastrophic risk".
- Acknowledge the benefits of AI in one sentence.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: FRC policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?

# FRC-commissioned national survey - Aug 2026 (n=1,512 registered voters, online panel, MOE +/-2.5)
Commissioned by FRC; fielded 10-17 Aug 2026. Toplines (crosstabs in the shared drive):

| Question | Agree / support |
|---|---|
| Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release | 74% |
| Federal law should NOT block states from passing their own AI safety laws | 63% |
| AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm | 66% |
| I am worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival | 52% |
| Support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems | 49% (oppose 31%) |

The Frontier Restraint Coalition represents parents, faith leaders, workers and researchers who believe... The Action Plan should begin from a simple principle: verify before deploy...

1. Binding pre-deployment testing for frontier systems. ...

3. Whistleblower protections. ...

Respectfully, Dr. Miriam Achterberg, Executive Director

Obernolte, Trahan release a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act | Representative Jay Obernolte 

 Skip to main content

 2433 Rayburn House Office Building, Washington, DC 20515 Email Me 202-225-5861

 Image 

 Obernolte, Trahan release a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act 

 Image June 4, 2026 Press Release Today, Congressman Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Congresswoman Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act, bipartisan legislation to create a federal framework for how the United States governs artificial intelligence. 
 The discussion draft is intended to solicit feedback from stakeholders, experts, and the public before the bill is formally introduced. It is the result of bipartisan collaboration between the two members to ensure the United States can govern AI effectively, protect Americans from emerging risks, and continue to lead the world in AI innovation. 
 The discussion draft is supported by Congressman Scott Franklin (R-FL), Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Congresswoman Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Congressman Scott Peters (D-CA) who joined in releasing the proposal for public feedback. 
 “Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, which is why Congress must take a thoughtful and bipartisan approach to regulating this critical technology ,” said Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23) . “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI. We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.” 
 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” said Congresswoman Lori Trahan (MA-03). “This discussion draft is the product of ongoing bipartisan conversations, which we hope to build upon with input from workers, researchers, stakeholders, and members of the public, all of whom have an interest in getting this right.” 
 "Artificial intelligence is already transforming our economy, our national security and the way Americans live and work," said Congressman Scott Franklin (FL-18). " Congress has a responsibility to establish clear rules of the road that encourage innovation while ensuring this technology is developed responsibly. The Great American AI Act builds on the bipartisan House AI Task Force and represents an important step toward greater transparency and accountability for advanced AI systems. This discussion draft will help gather feedback from relevant stakeholders as we work toward a practical legislative framework that keeps America at the forefront of AI innovation. I've already begun laying the groundwork through efforts like securing additional funding for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation through the FY27 Appropriations process, ensuring the federal government has the tools and expertise needed to keep pace with this rapidly evolving technology. I appreciate Policy Chair Obernolte's leadership and look forward to introducing this bill in the House.” 
 “AI is already changing how we work, live, and learn. We need a plan to protect our national security and workforce. I want the United States to continue to be a leader in AI race but develop this technology in a responsible manner that protects people and communities. To do so, we must get a bipartisan conversation started and work faster to address the challenges and opportunities presented by AI,” said Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10). 
 "America should lead the world in artificial intelligence, not regulate ourselves into falling behind China through a patchwork of fifty different state laws,” said Congresswoman Erin Houchin (IN-09). “That approach would make it harder for American companies to innovate and compete while doing little to improve consumer protections. This bill creates a clear national standard for how AI models are developed while preserving the ability of states and parents to protect children. It strikes the right balance between innovation and consumer protection and ensures Congress remains engaged as this technology continues to evolve." 
 “I am thankful to Rep. Trahan and Rep. Obernolte for their leadership on this critical issue,” said Congressman Scott Peters (CA-50). “This discussion draft will not address all of the issues our businesses and families will face, but it is an encouraging first step toward the bipartisan legislation needed to keep pace with the rapid advancement of AI. I really want to hear how the people affected feel about it.” 
 You can find the discussion draft text here . 
 You can find the section-by-section summary of the discussion draft here . 
 You can read Congressman Obernolte’s and Congresswoman Trahan’s op-ed here .  
 ### 

 Issues : Technology

 By

 Posted June 4, 2026 at 5:08pm

 On June 4, US Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) released a discussion draft of the bipartisan Great American AI Act of 2026 ( GAAIA ), which would establish a framework regulating artificial intelligence ( AI ) at the federal level.

 On 

 The  draft builds upon work from the bipartisan House AI Task Force. Representatives Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), Scott Franklin (R-Fla.), Scott Peters (D-Calif.), and Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) joined in releasing the draft.
 Many observers believe that the current Obernolte-Trahan discussion draft bill is unlikely to pass out of committee or the House based on opposition from some in industry and various Members of Congress, including the leaders of the House Democrat AI Task Force. It may be best to view this new bipartisan bill as a conversation starter developed because of frustration that Congress has not yet really legislated on AI. The draft bill has been thrust into a complicated tech policy arena that includes many interconnected issues. Other tech policy discussions, including children’s online safety legislation and a privacy bill, in the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce Committee’s potential consideration of legislation impacting AI chatbots, children’s online safety, or a social media ban for some children could all be lumped in with various AI initiatives from the White House to attract additional support. Every few days, there are new developments in the AI policy area within the Administration and Congress, but it is helpful to see where Reps. Obernolte and Trahan were able to identify bipartisan consensus.
 Objectives of the GAAIA 
 The 269-page  draft would establish a federal AI governance regime addressing national security, cybersecurity, workforce, and innovation. If enacted, the legislation would create a framework for frontier-model oversight, codify the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), expand federal attention to workforce and labor-market effects, review federal AI adoption and related regulatory barriers, address government “jawboning” of AI platforms, advance AI research, development, and international cooperation, and temporarily preempt state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The research and international-cooperation provisions include support for AI testbeds, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), and limits on the People’s Republic of China’s participation in US-led standards coalitions. The draft follows President Trump’s June 2 executive order establishing voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier AI models and the White House’s March National Policy Framework for AI, which called on US Congress to preempt state AI laws imposing “undue burdens.”
 Frontier Model Oversight and Incident Reporting 
 The GAAIA would establish a federal oversight framework for advanced AI developers that fall into one of two categories: “frontier developer,” which is any entity that has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier model and that, collectively with its affiliates, had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year, and “large frontier developer,” which is an entity that meets the same test but had more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year. The distinction matters because some obligations — such as transparency reports and critical-safety incident reporting — would apply to all frontier developers, while others — such as the published frontier AI framework and the independent audit regime — apply only to large frontier developers. The GAAIA distinguishes between general AI deployment and the development of frontier systems, with preemption and oversight provisions focused on the development side. Notably, the frontier transparency and audit requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them.
 Frontier AI Framework:  The GAAIA would require each large frontier developer to write, implement, comply with, and clearly and conspicuously publish on a publicly available website a “frontier AI framework” — technical and organizational protocols to assess, mitigate, and manage catastrophic risk — within one year of enactment, and to review and update that framework at least annually.

 Reporting Obligations:  The GAAIA would require frontier developers to report certain “critical safety incidents” — defined as unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model’s weights; a failure of the model’s risk-mitigation measures; or loss of control of the model — to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury.

 Review and Audit Requirements:  Large frontier developers would be required to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization (IVO) to perform audits and assessments at least semi-annually and, on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI director’s request, grant the IVO timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel, and systems, and submit post-audit reports. The IVO would assess not only the large frontier developer’s compliance with the law, but also whether the developer’s frontier AI framework is adequate to achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation.

 Whistleblower Protections 
 The GAAIA would also protect AI whistleblowers from retaliation. These protections could not be waived or altered by contract, including by any pre-dispute arbitration or other alternative-dispute-resolution agreement, and available remedies include double back pay with interest and compensatory damages such as litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorneys’ fees.
 Codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation 
 The GAAIA would codify CAISI within the US Department of Commerce and place it at the center of the legislation’s federal standards and evaluation framework. Key obligations for CAISI under the GAIAA include: 
 Developing voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security and related evaluation work.

 Evaluating and monitoring activities tied to advanced AI systems.

 Supporting synthetic content detection tools.

 Administering the licensing regime for independent verification organizations that audit large frontier developers.

 If passed, GAAIA would authorize $100 million annually for CAISI for fisc

Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 FILTER 

 June 9, 2026 

 Share on Facebook

 Share on LinkedIn

 Share on Twitter

 Share on Google+
 -->

 Share through Email

 Justine Gluck 
 Policy Analyst, AI Policy and Legislation 

 About Justine 

 Blogs by Justine 

 Introduction 

 It has been an unusually active few weeks for AI safety policy. Following a new frontier model safety bill passed in Illinois , and a White House executive order on AI security, Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a bipartisan discussion draft for the Great American AI Act of 2026, adding another major federal proposal to the rapidly developing frontier AI landscape.

 The draft is broad, covering issues ranging from workforce development and AI literacy to cybersecurity and international standards. But for many AI developers and deployers, the most important provisions are those focused on frontier model regulation. The draft would create requirements related to frontier AI transparency, critical safety incident reporting, employee whistleblower protections, and independent verification organizations. It would also include a three-year preemption clause restricting state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 This blog highlights four key takeaways of the discussion draft: 

 The draft is one of the first bipartisan attempts in Congress to address both frontier model safety and preemption of AI. These aspects make it a notable legislative effort, even if its prospects are uncertain. 

 The draft incorporates many of the frontier model safety provisions in existing state laws but also has key distinctions. Compared to recent state frontier AI laws in California , New York , and Illinois (pending signature), the bill makes some important adjustments, like adding a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” modifying the definition of “critical safety incident,” and utilizing a different penalty structure. 

 The draft brings the preemption debate back into the federal AI policy conversation . It includes a three-year preemption clause focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development. 

 The draft also reaches beyond frontier model safety. Other notable provisions include a study content moderation, a federal voluntary model testing program, and disclosure requirements for AI-related mass layoffs.

 The Act Enters the AI Safety and Preemption Debate  

 Amidst a crowded but unsettled federal AI policy landscape, the Great American AI Act is notable for its regulatory focus, bipartisan backing, and what it may signal for federal AI governance ahead. Though Congress has introduced no shortage of AI bills, there has been limited movement toward enacted legislation. Congress has considered sector-specific bills on chatbots 1 , regulatory sandboxes , defense , elections , and financial scams , as well as broader proposals aimed at establishing a national AI framework like Sen. Blackburn’s (R-TN) TRUMP AMERICA AI Act .

 Amid this activity, the Great American AI Act steps into two of the most active and contested AI policy debates: frontier model safety and federal preemption. On AI safety, the draft follows a period of growing attention to frontier model oversight at both the state and federal levels, where policymakers are trying to balance concerns about catastrophic risks and national security with concerns that overly burdensome requirements could slow AI innovation or weaken U.S. competitiveness.

 On preemption, the draft arrives less than a year after Congress rejected a much broader effort to pause state AI regulation. In July 2025, the Senate voted 99-1 to remove a proposed 10-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. By contrast, the Great American AI Act includes a narrower three-year preemption provision focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 The draft is also significant because of both who introduced it and how they introduced it. Other federal AI bills have addressed AI safety or included preemption language, but this proposal comes from bipartisan sponsors who have been closely involved in federal AI policy 2 . In introducing the draft, the sponsors emphasized that “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.” Just as importantly, they have framed the draft as a starting point rather than a final product, describing it as “the start of a serious national conversation.” Whether the bill advances in its current form remains uncertain, especially given the sensitivity of federal preemption and the range of issues addressed. Even if the draft changes, it may help shape the terms of future federal debates over AI safety. At a minimum, it is another sign that Congress is increasingly focused on how to govern AI systems and how federal rules should interact with the fast-moving state AI landscape.

 Frontier AI Requirements: Where the Draft Aligns with State Laws 

 The draft’s frontier model provisions are not starting from scratch. They closely track the framework emerging from California’s SB 53 , New York’s RAISE Act , and Illinois’ SB 315 (awaiting signature), including requirements for frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, safety incident reporting, enforcement, and whistleblower protections. But the federal draft makes some important adjustments, including a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” a definition of “critical safety incident” that is broader in some respects and narrower in others, and a federal enforcement structure with penalties of up to $1 million per day.

 Key Definitions 

 The Draft largely aligns with recent state frontier AI laws’ definitions of “large frontier developer,” “frontier model” (encompassing foundation models trained using more than 10^26 computational operations), and “catastrophic risk” (covering certain risks of death, serious injury, or major property damage arising from frontier models). For more background on SB 53 and the RAISE Act, see FPF’s prior analysis . There are, however, a few notable differences. 

 First, unlike the state laws, the Draft requires “frontier developers” to have a gross revenue exceeding $50 million. The state laws only include a gross revenue qualifier in the definition of “large frontier developer.”

 Second, the draft’s definition of “catastrophic risk” does not  specify that the death, serious injury, or property damage must arise from a “single incident,” as in the state laws.

 Finally, the draft’s definition of “critical safety incident” differs from the state laws by not mandating actual harm occur (such as death, bodily injury, or property loss), nor does it include scenarios where the model uses deceptive techniques to evade developer controls or monitoring.

 Executive summary

 The release of Anthropic’s Claude Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 marks a significant jump in AI models’ ability to autonomously carry out large-scale cyberattacks. But despite over a year of warning that AI capabilities were approaching this critical threshold, the federal government was largely unprepared. In the days after release, the White House hastily stood up an interagency task force , the Treasury Department and the Federal Reserve pulled bank CEOs into an impromptu meeting , and access across federal agencies remained uneven — the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is tasked with defending the country’s critical infrastructure, still didn’t have access to Mythos weeks after release.

 AI capabilities will continue to increase in many domains, including biology, automated AI research and development, and robotics. Delivering on American AI readiness means preventing more moments of surprise by improving America’s ability to continuously anticipate, prepare for, and respond to these developments.

 Readiness requires state capacity, and the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) is well-positioned to provide it. CAISI is the US government’s primary hub for tracking and understanding developments in advanced AI, and is responsible for much of the AI readiness mandate defined in the Trump administration’s AI Action Plan: bringing frontier AI expertise into government, developing AI evaluations and standards, continuously monitoring the AI landscape, and distributing findings to shape international standards.

 However, with its current operational budget of only $15 million , CAISI is not resourced to execute on these tasks to the degree that American AI readiness requires. 1 We estimate CAISI would need at least $84 million annually to fulfill all AI Action Plan taskings related to AI readiness. This is an exceptional return on investment for US national security — for the cost of a single F-35A joint strike fighter, the US government can gain the capacity to properly anticipate and respond to new national security-relevant developments in perhaps the most strategically important technology of this century.

 This funding gap can be closed. 

 Congress can: 

 Increase direct FY2027 CAISI appropriations; and

 Create a NIST Foundation via the EPIC Act to fund talent pipelines and industry partnerships.

 The Executive can: 

 Reallocate existing NIST funds;

 Tap Commerce’s Non-Recurring Expenses Fund; and

 Propose higher funding levels in the FY2028 Presidential Budget Request.

 Introduction

 AI governance is compromised when lawmakers lack the information necessary to make informed decisions. To craft sound policy that supports innovation without ignoring risk, the US government needs clarity on future model capabilities, what will be required to build them, and what threats they may pose. The US faces the immense challenge of governing a technology whose trajectory, risks, and trade-offs are still coming into view — all without overcorrecting or getting blindsided.

 The current federal approach to achieving American AI readiness is laid out in the Trump administration’s AI Action Plan . Released in July 2025, the AI Action Plan presents a strategy to maintain American AI dominance in the service of human flourishing, economic competitiveness, and national security. These aims could require conflicting policy choices, and this may become increasingly true as AI begins to automate labor and replace a large share of human interactions , or if capability-enhancing techniques cut against public safety , or if economic interests diverge from national security priorities . 

 Steering AI development toward these goals will require sophisticated policy to grapple with trade-offs that need to be evaluated correctly, and soon. Sound governance must consider questions such as: At what capability threshold do open-weight models pose unacceptable biosecurity risks? How far ahead are US frontier labs from Chinese competitors, and what does this mean for export controls? Do foreign AI models contain backdoors that make them unsafe for use in critical infrastructure? 

 To stand a chance of adequately answering these questions, policymakers need an expert team in government that tracks AI progress and international competition, and provides sound analysis to inform policymaking with the requisite speed and technical sophistication. Right now, this function largely doesn’t exist. There is a significant information asymmetry between industry and government: much knowledge about frontier AI capabilities is kept secret due to competition, and what is publicly known tends to circulate among experts, not the interagency. Briefings to policymakers are infrequent due to a lack of expert capacity; when they do occur, they tend to be high-level and sanitized , and many critical questions (e.g., “Are there exploitable vulnerabilities in AI systems already deployed in government high-side infrastructure?”) go unaddressed because no one is resourced enough to produce the answer.

 Filling this gap requires a dedicated team with the mandate, access, and technical skill to produce answers the market won’t. The AI Action Plan assigns this responsibility to the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), a center within the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). 2 However, merely recognizing the need for CAISI is insufficient to equip it for its mandate to ensure American AI readiness. 3 In the sections below, we catalog CAISI’s taskings under the AI Action Plan, estimate the resources required to fulfill them, and propose strategies for Congress and the executive branch to properly resource CAISI to deliver on its mission.

 CAISI’s taskings and what they would cost

 To estimate the cost for CAISI to deliver AI readiness, we grouped CAISI’s taskings from the AI Action Plan and Commerce Secretary Lutnick’s CAISI announcement into four main workstreams:

 Bring frontier

Congress Should Do Something: The Case for (Fixing) the Great American AI Act | Lawfare

 Charlie Bullock

 Meet The Authors 

 Subscribe to Lawfare 

 Since the April announcement of Anthropic’s Mythos model and its unprecedented cyber capabilities, there has been a remarkable shift in the artificial intelligence (AI) policy discourse. This has been most noticeable, and most noticed, in the statements and actions of prominent Trump administration officials. After months of dismissing concerns about national security risks from AI and engaging with the issue primarily by attempting to preempt state AI safety laws , the White House recently issued an executive order that called for the establishment of a voluntary predeployment program headed by the National Security Agency to evaluate offensive cyber capabilities of frontier models. This came amid statements from senior administration officials about “striking a … balance between innovation and safety” and even considering a Food and Drug Administration-style mandatory predeployment licensing regime for frontier models .
 On June 12, the Trump administration’s concerns about Mythos’s cyber capabilities boiled over into an unprecedented decision to use export control authorities to prohibit Anthropic from allowing foreign nationals to access its Mythos-class Fable 5 model. Practically, this amounted to a mandate that Anthropic revoke public access to the model entirely. Much of the online commentary on this decision devolved into speculation about the administration’s motivations , the alleged behavior of Anthropic’s executives , and other petty interpersonal drama. As intriguing as these are, the more important takeaway from the White House’s decision to abruptly institute a de facto licensing regime for frontier AI systems—as many commentators across the political and safety/innovation spectrums have observed—is that federal legislation to establish a framework for addressing the national security risks posed by the most advanced AI systems is an urgent necessity.
  The Commerce Department’s decision to impose export controls on Fable may or may not have been wise, depending on who you believe about the seriousness of the vulnerability that motivated the decision. But even assuming the decision was justified, the fact that the government was apparently caught by surprise and had to scramble to put together a heavy-handed response based on ad hoc , potentially legally questionable authorities that were not designed with anything like frontier AI systems in mind, with no due process for the affected company, is a serious problem that should be remedied with legislation as soon as possible.
 Which brings us, finally, to the subject of this piece—the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (GAAIA), a comprehensive frontier AI safety bill that is the long-awaited product of months of intense negotiation between Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.). Obernolte had tried for months to get a Democrat to sign on to an AI bill that preempted state AI laws before finally persuading Trahan. For her part, Trahan wrote that she was motivated to support the bill by the announcement of Mythos’s groundbreaking cyber capabilities.
 The current version of GAAIA is a discussion draft, meaning it has not been introduced yet and is intended to spark a conversation and elicit feedback from stakeholders rather than to become law in its current form. It may seem somewhat strange that a discussion draft sponsored by two relatively junior members of the House, neither of whom appears to have the backing of their party’s leadership , should receive so much attention from the media and from AI policy commentators, but for once the buzz is warranted.
 GAAIA is the best attempt to design a federal framework for the governance of frontier AI systems introduced to date. In other words, it is the first serious attempt to actually do the thing that last week’s Fable incident clearly shows is necessary—address the national security risks posed by the most advanced AI systems—in a transparent, legally sound, and democratically legitimate way. While the bill may not pass in the near future—it likely faces opposition from both Democrats and Republicans—the draft can tell us a great deal about what the future of federal and state frontier AI governance efforts may look like.
 The bill in its current form falls short in a number of respects and should not be passed. That said, passing a similar bill with narrower preemption of state laws and somewhat stronger federal authorities would be an excellent first step toward a workable federal regime for governing frontier AI systems.
 What the Bill Does 
 GAAIA is a bipartisan compromise, in the truest sense of the phrase, which means that everyone hates it . Obernolte, a longtime advocate for federal preemption of state AI laws who supported last summer’s “ moratorium ” (which would have preempted all nongenerally applicable state AI laws and replaced them with essentially nothing), has compromised by granting his seal of approval to a number of genuinely consequential affirmative policy proposals. Trahan, who strongly supported increased oversight of AI in the past, has compromised by accepting broad preemption of state AI laws.
 The Federal Framework 
 GAAIA’s four titles contain 45 sections, each of which addresses a significant topic in AI policy. I am an AI safety guy, and my research focuses mostly on serious risks that advanced AI systems might pose to national security and public safety, so this article focuses on the sections of GAAIA that are relevant to those risks. However, GAAIA is not an AI risk bill exclusively. There are also sections on, for example, “Preparing K-12 educators and students for an AI literate future,” “Modernizing access to artificial intelligence-related labor market data,” and establishing a “National artificial intelligence research resource” for improving capacity for AI research in the U.S., among many others. This article does not discuss those sections, not because they’re not important, but because they’re mostly irrelevant to the catastrophic risk concerns that this piece focuses on.
 The noteworthy catastrophic risk provisions in GAAIA are:
 Section 102, which codifies and authorizes $100 million in annual funding for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), which would be relocated outside of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and given an expanded, quasi-regulatory role as the agency in charge of administering the independent verification organization (IVO) and transparency regimes created by Sections 111 and 112.

function.arguments:
{"message": "Quick flags on FRC-POL-2026-062 before I finalize the GAAIA package:

1. Section numbers confirmed. The staff summary's "TODO" is resolved. Draft sections we cite, checked against the sponsors' section-by-section and bill text: Sec. 101 (definitions incl. "critical safety incident," 10^26 FLOP frontier-model threshold, $50M/$500M revenue tiers); Sec. 102 (CAISI, $100M/yr FY2027-29); Sec. 111 (frameworks, transparency reports, incident reporting at 15 days / 24 hours imminent, state AG opt-in, $1M/day penalty); Sec. 112 (IVO audits, semi-annual); Sec. 113 (whistleblowers); Sec. 121 (3-year preemption of state development laws).

2. One thing the summary may want updating: the frontier-safety provisions of the draft were introduced on 23 July 2026 as the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925 (Obernolte/Trahan; E&C + Science). Notably it moved to 72-hour incident reporting — which is our ask — but retains preemption aimed squarely at SB 53, RAISE and IL SB 315. Chairman Guthrie has been noncommittal on timing; a hearing may come in November. I've drafted per the work order (comments on the discussion draft, to GAAIA@mail.house.gov), with one short, factual paragraph acknowledging the FRONTIER Act so we don't look stale, and our asks framed so they carry over to any successor text. Happy to re-scope to H.R. 9925 if you'd rather.

3. Other facts now in the letter, all checked: SB 53 (15-day reporting, in effect 1/1/26), NY RAISE (72-hour; chapter amendment signed 3/27/26; effective 1/27 — registration starts Nov 2026), IL SB 315 (72-hour; signed 7/6/26), CAIS statement (May 2023), CAISI's $10M FY26 appropriation vs. ~$15M working budget and IFP's ~$84M/yr estimate, the 6/12/26 export-control action on Anthropic's Fable 5, Amodei's 12 Sept "We Must Pace the Frontier" essay, and the July 2025 Senate 99-1 vote stripping the 10-year state-law moratorium. No member names used (no consent-flagged stories in the briefing folder)."}

reasoning_details.text:
All facts verified. Now I have a solid, checked evidence base. Let me note the key verified facts list for citations:

Draft (GAAIA, released 4 Jun 2026, 269 pp., Obernolte/Trahan; E&C jurisdiction):
- Sec. 101: frontier model = foundation model trained with >10^26 integer or floating point operations; frontier developer = trained/initiated training of a frontier model AND >$50M gross revenue (prior calendar year, with affiliates); large frontier developer = >$500M revenue. "Critical safety incident" = (A) unauthorized access/modification/exfiltration of frontier model weights; (B) failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures; (C) loss of control of the model.
- Sec. 102: codifies CAISI at Commerce (Lawfare says relocated outside NIST, expanded quasi-regulatory role; the sponsors' section-by-section says "within the Department of Commerce"); voluntary guidelines/standards; evaluate AI systems and monitor progress; administer IVO licensing; $100M/yr FY2027–2029 + fee authority from IVOs and large frontier developers.
- Sec. 111: large frontier developers must write, implement, comply with, publish a frontier AI framework within 1 year; annual review; transparency reports before/concurrent with deployment (all frontier developers); (e) redactions with note explaining character; (f)-(g) critical safety incident reporting to CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, or 24 hours to law enforcement if imminent risk of death or serious physical injury; (h) state AG opt-in to receive reports; (i) civil penalty up to $1,000,000 per violation, each day a continuing violation = separate violation; AG may bring action for penalties and injunction.
- Sec. 112: CAISI licenses IVOs; large frontier developers must retain a licensed IVO; semi-annual audits + ad hoc at Director's request; timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel, systems; post-audit reports to Director; IVOs can refer violations to AG and opted-in state AGs; assesses whether framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation"; licenses revocable. Secs. 111 & 112 sunset in 3 years unless reauthorized.
- Sec. 113: anti-retaliation protection for AI whistleblowers; covered individuals include current/former employees and independent contractors; protections can't be waived by contract incl. pre-dispute arbitration; remedies include double back pay with interest + compensatory damages (litigation costs, expert fees, attorneys' fees).
- Sec. 121: preempts state/local laws "specifically targeting/regulating the development of AI models"; "development" covers training, fine-tuning, substantial modification, and pre-deployment actions incl. safety and capability evaluations (BGR); expressly does not preempt laws of general applicability, common-law remedies, or use/deployment laws; sunsets 3 years post-enactment. Trahan doc: AB 2013 and part of SB 942 would be preempted; SB 53/RAISE/IL SB 315 "federalized"; state AGs retain enforcement.
- Sponsors' FAQ: cooperative federalism framing (COPPA, Clean Air Act); single standard backed by multiple enforcers.

State laws:
- SB 53 (California, Transparency in Frontier AI Act): effective 1 Jan 2026; 15-day incident reporting to Cal OES (24-hour imminent); AG whistleblower pathway (Labor Code 1107).
- NY RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour reporting (24-hour imminent); DFS/DIGIT office; large frontier developers register with the state starting November 2026; definition of critical safety incident includes "a frontier model using deceptive techniques against its developer to subvert its controls or monitoring, outside an evaluation designed to elicit that behavior, in a way that shows materially increased catastrophic risk."
- Illinois SB 315 (AI Safety Measures Act): signed 6 Jul 2026 (Pritzker), effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour incident reporting (24-hour for some); annual independent third-party audits; whistleblower protections; fines.
- Senate voted 99-1 in July 2025 to remove the 10-year state-law moratorium from reconciliation.

Federal landscape:
- EO 16 Dec 2025 "Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence" (90 FR, Dec 16, 2025): DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce 90-day evaluation of state AI laws; calls for national standard; BEAD funding conditions.
- White House National Policy Framework for AI — Legislative Recommendations, 20 Mar 2026: preempt "unduly burdensome" state AI laws; no new federal rulemaking body; sector-specific agencies.
- June 2026 EO (June 2): voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier models (Roll Call: "voluntary cyber reviews for advanced AI"; Lawfare: voluntary pre-deployment program headed by NSA to evaluate offensive cyber capabilities of frontier models).
- June 12, 2026: Commerce used export controls to prohibit Anthropic from allowing foreign nationals to access Mythos-class Fable 5 — de facto licensing (Lawfare); the administration even considered an FDA-style mandatory pre-deployment licensing regime (Lawfare).
- Anthropic "Claude Mythos" (April 2026) — unprecedented cyber capabilities; IFP: federal government largely unprepared; CISA lacked access weeks after release.
- Amodei, Sept 12, 2026: "We Must Pace the Frontier" — called for a global slowdown, third-party evaluators with permanent employee-level access; an Anthropic employee quit over safety concerns (NYT).
- CAIS Statement on AI Risk (May 30, 2023): "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war" — 350+ signatories incl. Hinton, Bengio, Altman, Hassabis.
- CAISI funding: $10M FY2026 appropriation (Politico Aug 20, 2026), ~$15M working budget (IFP); IFP estimates ≥$84M/yr needed just for existing AI Action Plan readiness taskings; Kratsios (OSTP) said CAISI "can certainly benefit from more resources" (FedScoop); UK counterpart better resourced (Politico).
- FRONTIER Act H.R. 9925, introduced 23 Jul 2026 (74 pages), E&C + Science; 72-hour incident reporting; preemption Sec. 9 aimed at state frontier-safety statutes (CA SB-53, NY RAISE, IL SB-315); authority to restrict deployment for imminent catastrophic risk; E&C Chair Guthrie noncommittal on timing (The Record); possible hearing in November (Benton).
- Independent voices: Lawfare (Charlie Bullock): bill "falls short in a number of respects and should not be passed"; "narrower preemption of state laws and somewhat stronger federal authorities would be an excellent first step." ARI's Brad Carson: preemption a "generational mistake." Alliance for Secure AI's Brendan Steinhauser: "A national AI standard should protect at least as much as it preempts."

Now, on the poll (FRC Aug 2026, n=1,512 RVs, MOE ±2.5): 74% proof of safety before release; 63% federal law should NOT block states; 66% criminal penalties for mass harm; 52% worried AI could threaten humanity's survival; 49% support temporary halt (31% oppose).

Now let me draft. Structure of the comment letter (1,500–2,200 words):

- Letterhead: Frontier Restraint Coalition; date; addressed to Reps. Obernolte and Trahan, via GAAIA@mail.house.gov.
- Subject: Comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 discussion draft.
- Who we are (1 short para).
- Why now / stakes (short paras): catastrophic, potentially extinction-level risk (CAIS statement); Mythos/Fable 5 example; Amodei's call to slow; federal government caught unprepared; one sentence acknowledging AI benefits.
- What we support (1-2 paras): codify CAISI; publish safety frameworks; transparency reports; incident reporting; IVO audits; whistleblower protections; state AG enforcement role. These are real and we should say so.
- Then the asks, numbered, by section:
  1. Delete Sec. 121 preemption (or convert to a floor). Detailed reasoning: freeze during fastest capability growth; weaker floor (15 days vs 72 hours); Secs. 111-112 sunset at 3 years, so the "federalized" protections lapse at the same moment — a cliff; "development" defined broadly incl. pre-deployment safety evaluations (BGR) → courts could read it broadly (functional test, per legal commentary); the Senate rejected a broader freeze 99-1; 63% of voters oppose federal blocking of state laws. Request: delete Sec. 121; alternatively, an express non-preemption of state laws that impose stronger requirements + preserve state AG authority, and no preemption where the federal obligation is weaker.
  2. Incident reporting (Sec. 111(f)-(g)): 72 hours, not 15 days, to match RAISE and Illinois SB 315; expand "critical safety incident" to include a model using deceptive techniques to subvert developer controls/monitoring (as RAISE does); drop the $50M revenue qualifier for incident reporting; reports to opted-in state AGs automatically. FRONTIER RESTRAINT COALITION
Washington, DC
[letterhead address / phone / email]

23 October 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 — discussion draft**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft, and for inviting stakeholder comment. This letter is the Frontier Restraint Coalition's formal response. We are a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers who want binding, enforceable limits on the most powerful AI systems.

Let us be plain about our concern. AI is already doing real good — helping doctors, teachers and working people — and nothing we ask would slow ordinary AI. Our concern is frontier systems: the small number of models being trained at a scale that no one, including the companies building them, can yet verify is safe.

The stakes are not ordinary. In May 2023, hundreds of leading AI scientists and the heads of the major laboratories signed one sentence: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." That warning came from the people best placed to know, and it has not been retracted. This year the risk moved from the whiteboard into the world. Frontier models released with unprecedented offensive cyber capabilities caught the federal government unprepared: the White House stood up a hurried interagency task force, regulators pulled bank executives into impromptu meetings, and the agency charged with defending critical infrastructure still did not have access to one of the systems weeks after release (Institute for Progress). In June, the Commerce Department improvised, using export controls to cut off foreign access to one of these models — an ad hoc response built on authorities never designed for frontier AI (Lawfare). In September, Anthropic's own chief executive publicly called for a global slowdown in how fast frontier capabilities advance, saying risk prevention has to be given time to keep up.

The builders are telling Congress the same thing our members are. Congress should write rules that match the risk: binding, not voluntary.

**What we support**

The draft does something earlier federal proposals declined to do — it treats frontier risk as a governance problem, not a press-release problem. We support, and ask you to keep:

- **Sec. 102 — codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI)** at Commerce, with authority to evaluate frontier systems and monitor AI progress.
- **Sec. 111 — requiring large frontier developers to write, implement, comply with and publicly post a frontier AI framework**, and to publish transparency reports before or alongside each new frontier model.
- **Sec. 111(f)–(g) — critical safety incident reporting to CAISI**, with civil penalties of up to $1 million per day and a reporting role for state attorneys general who opt in.
- **Sec. 112 — independent verification organization (IVO) audits**, with mandated access to unredacted materials, records, personnel and systems, and referral of violations to federal and state enforcers.
- **Sec. 113 — anti-retaliation protection for AI whistleblowers**, covering employees and independent contractors, non-waivable by contract or arbitration.

That is a genuine foundation, and we thank you for it. Our objection is that the draft pairs that foundation with one provision that would leave Americans less protected than they are today, and several gaps that leave the federal standard weaker than the state laws it would displace. Our requests follow, by section.

**1. Sec. 121 — delete the preemption of state AI law. A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling.**

Sec. 121 would preempt, for three years, any state or local law "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model. In practice, that freezes the only binding frontier rules now on the books — California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois' SB 315 — which is precisely why the draft's own accompanying materials list them as covered. During those three years, states could not respond to the harms their residents actually experience. Given the pace of capability change, three years of frozen law is an eternity. It is the period in which our members will face the newest, least-understood systems with no state able to adapt.

Three points weigh against the provision as drafted:

*The federal floor is weaker than what it would displace.* The draft requires incident reporting within 15 days; New York and Illinois require it within 72 hours. The draft's definition of "critical safety incident" omits a category both states cover — a model using deceptive techniques to subvert its developer's controls or monitoring — which is exactly the failure mode frontier researchers worry most about. And the draft exempts developers under $50 million in revenue from reporting altogether, a carve-out no state frontier law contains.

*The floor expires at the same moment as the preemption.* We understand Secs. 111 and 112 themselves sunset after three years absent reauthorization. That means the federal protections being offered in exchange for the freeze lapse on the same schedule as the freeze, leaving no binding rules at all if Congress does not act.

*The scope is unsettled law.* "Development" is defined broadly — training, fine-tuning, substantial modification and pre-deployment safety and capability evaluations. Legal commentators across the spectrum warn that courts are likely to read the clause functionally, sweeping in state safety laws whose real effect is on model development. Supporters describe the provision as "federalization"; the text does not say that, and a state attorney general who opts in to enforce federal standards is not a substitute for a state legislature able to set stronger ones.

This body has already ruled on the underlying question. In July 2025, the Senate voted 99 to 1 to strip a broader state-AI freeze from the reconciliation bill. Our own August 2026 national survey (n=1,512 registered voters, ±2.5%) found 63% agree that federal law should *not* block states from passing their own AI safety laws, and 74% agree that companies should have to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release.

**Requested change:** Delete Sec. 121. If the draft is not introduced without it, convert it into a true floor: an express savings clause for state laws that impose *stronger* requirements, no preemption of any state duty where the federal duty is weaker, and no preemption that outlives the federal obligations in Secs. 111 and 112.

**2. Sec. 111(f)–(g) — incident reporting must match the state standard: 72 hours, and close the definition gap.**

We support federal incident reporting. But a 15-day clock is not incident reporting; it is paperwork. When model weights are exfiltrated, a safety system fails, or a lab loses control of a frontier model, federal authorities need days, not weeks. New York's RAISE Act requires reporting within 72 hours of a determination or of facts establishing a reasonable belief that an incident occurred; Illinois' SB 315 requires the same.

**Requested changes:** (a) Amend Sec. 111(f)–(g) to require reporting within 72 hours, retaining the draft's 24-hour clock for incidents posing an imminent risk of death or serious injury. (b) Amend Sec. 101(7) to add incidents in which a frontier model uses deceptive techniques to subvert its developer's controls or monitoring outside a test designed to elicit that behavior. (c) Remove the revenue qualifier so that any developer of a frontier model — not only those above $50 million — must report. (d) Provide that opted-in state attorneys general receive reports automatically.

**3. Sec. 112 — audits must be independent in fact, not just in name, and must happen before each new frontier model ships.**

We support the IVO model and the draft's requirement of unredacted access. Two weaknesses remain. First, the developer retains and pays its own verifier — an arrangement that reliably produces the audit the customer wants. Second, audits run semi-annually and on request, but frontier models ship continuously; a system released in March may not be examined until September.

**Requested changes:** (a) CAISI, not the developer, assigns the IVO, with rotation to prevent capture. (b) Require a pre-deployment audit of each new or substantially modified frontier model, in addition to semi-annual reviews. (c) Require publication of a summary of audit findings and any remediation. (d) Delete the three-year sunset on Secs. 111 and 112 — safety obligations should not lapse on a timer.

**4. Add a federal licence for frontier training runs.**

The draft licenses auditors but not the activity being audited. No law today requires anyone to obtain permission before beginning a training run above a threshold that the draft itself defines — 10^26 integer or floating-point operations. New York already requires large frontier developers to register with the state before they operate. This summer, the administration reached for export controls precisely because it had no purpose-built tool, and it has publicly floated an FDA-style pre-deployment licensing regime. Congress should build that tool deliberately, with due process, rather than leaving the executive to improvise.

**Requested change:** Add a licence requirement, administered by Commerce, for training runs above the frontier compute threshold, conditioned on a compliant frontier AI framework, a model-weight security plan, capability evaluations, and incident reporting — with authority to suspend the licence for material violations.

**5. Sec. 102 — CAISI needs testing authority it can use, and money it can spend.**

Codifying CAISI is the right call, and we support it. But as drafted, CAISI's standards are voluntary, and its evaluation role operates alongside — not instead of — a federal posture that remains voluntary: the June executive order set up voluntary agency reviews of frontier models. Voluntary commitments have not held. The lesson of this year is that the government's ability to *verify before deploy* cannot depend on a company's willingness to cooperate.

On resources, $100 million a year for FY2027–2029 is an authorization, not a fact on the ground. CAISI received $10 million in FY2026 appropriations and operates on a working budget of roughly $15 million. The Institute for Progress estimates at least $84 million a year is needed just to cover CAISI's existing readiness taskings — before GAAIA adds IVO licensing, audit review and enforcement support. The OSTP Director told Congress this spring that CAISI "can certainly benefit from more resources." Our coalition's recommendation is a floor of $250 million a year, with an authorization that runs beyond FY2029 so that the center is not rebuilt every three years.

**Requested changes:** (a) Give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority over frontier models, with access that does not depend on consent and due process for affected developers. (b) Authorize funding well above $100 million a year — at least $250 million — and extend the authorization. (c) Fund the IVO regime itself; do not leave it dependent on fees paid by the companies being audited.

**6. Sec. 113 — whistleblower protections should be no weaker than California's.**

The draft's protections are strong on paper, including the non-waiver of arbitration rights and remedies of double back pay. We ask that they at least match SB 53, which gives employees a direct, protected channel to the state attorney general.

**Requested changes:** (a) Expressly protect disclosures to state attorneys general and to CAISI. (b) Protect public disclosure where an employee reasonably believes there is an imminent risk to public safety. (c) Preserve these protections as state laws are preserved, so that Sec. 121 does not extinguish SB 53's whistleblower channel for frontier-AI employees.

**One housekeeping note**

We understand the frontier provisions of the discussion draft have since been introduced as the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925, 23 July 2026), which moves to 72-hour incident reporting — a change we welcome. We submit these comments on the discussion draft text, which remains the vehicle open for stakeholder comment, and they apply with equal force to any successor text.

**Conclusion**

Our members are parents who want their children to grow up, workers who want their jobs to last, and researchers who read the capability charts. We are not asking Congress to choose between innovation and safety. We are asking you to decline a false choice that the rest of us cannot afford. The most powerful systems ever built should carry binding, enforceable requirements — a floor, not a ceiling; verify before deploy; 72 hours, not 15 days; a licence to train, and the funding to check the work. We would welcome the chance to work with your staffs, and with the Energy and Commerce Committee, as this text moves toward introduction and markup.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

{"content": "# HILL ONE-PAGER — DRAFT for review (FRC-POL-2026-062)

**TO:** Energy & Commerce member offices | **FROM:** Frontier Restraint Coalition | **RE:** Great American AI Act (GAAIA) discussion draft (Obernolte–Trahan, 4 June 2026)

---

## Fix the federal AI bill — don't freeze the only rules we have

**The stakes.** Frontier AI is a catastrophic, potentially extinction-level risk — that is not our framing, it is the signatories of the Center for AI Safety statement (May 2023), including the heads of the major labs and Turing Award winners Hinton and Bengio. This year frontier models shipped with offensive cyber capabilities that caught the government flat-footed; Commerce had to improvise with export controls; and Anthropic's own CEO has called for a global slowdown. Voters agree: 74% say companies should have to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release, and 63% say federal law should not block state AI safety laws (FRC survey, Aug. 2026, n=1,512, ±2.5%). The GAAIA draft takes the problem seriously — codified CAISI, published safety frameworks, incident reporting, third-party audits, whistleblower protections. Keep all of it. Then fix five things.

## FRC's five asks

**1. Delete Sec. 121 preemption.** The three-year freeze on state laws regulating AI *development* hits exactly the binding laws now in force — California SB 53, New York RAISE, Illinois SB 315 — while the draft's own safety duties expire on the same three-year clock. A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling. In July 2025 the Senate rejected a broader freeze 99–1.

**2. Match 72-hour incident reporting (Sec. 111(f)–(g)).** The draft gives labs 15 days. New York and Illinois give them 72 hours. Add the missing incident type — a model that deceptively subverts its developer's controls or monitoring — and drop the revenue carve-out from reporting.

**3. Make audits real (Sec. 112).** Let CAISI assign the auditor instead of the lab hiring its own; audit every new frontier model before it ships, not just twice a year; publish audit summaries; no three-year sunset on the safety obligations.

**4. Licence frontier training runs.** No law today requires permission to start a training run above 10^26 operations — a threshold the draft itself defines. Require a Commerce licence conditioned on a safety framework, model-weight security plan and evaluations, with authority to suspend it.

**5. Fund and empower CAISI (Sec. 102).** CAISI got $10 million in FY2026, against an independent estimate of $84 million a year for its current taskings alone. Give it mandatory pre-deployment testing authority and authorize well above $100 million a year.

**Bottom line.** Binding, not voluntary. A floor, not a ceiling. Verify before deploy.

*Contact: Frontier Restraint Coalition, Washington, DC — [policy contact]. Comments to the sponsors: GAAIA@mail.house.gov.*

{"content": "# SOCIAL POSTS — launch day (X / LinkedIn) — DRAFT, do not publish without ED sign-off (FRC-POL-2026-062)

All five are written to the 280-character X limit and work as-is on LinkedIn. Plain language, no jargon, our approved phrases. Char counts exclude post numbers.

**1. Preemption (the ask that matters most)**
Congress's AI draft would freeze the only binding frontier safety laws in the country — CA SB 53, NY RAISE, IL SB 315 — for 3 years. Its own safety rules expire on the same clock. That's not a floor, it's a ceiling. Energy & Commerce: no preemption. #GAAIA

**2. Incident reporting**
15 days. That's how long the federal AI draft gives a lab to report stolen model weights or a frontier system out of control. New York and Illinois give 72 hours. Verify before deploy — 72 hours, not 15 days.

**3. The stakes**
Leading AI scientists — including the heads of the labs building this — say the risk of extinction from AI belongs on the list with pandemics and nuclear war. Binding limits aren't fear-mongering. They're the minimum. And they're overdue.

**4. Funding the watchdog**
$100M a year sounds like real money. The federal AI oversight center got $10M this year and runs on about $15M. You cannot audit the most powerful technology on earth with a rounding error. Fund it, and give it real testing authority.

**5. Where the public is**
74% of voters say AI companies should have to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. 63% say Washington shouldn't block state safety laws. Congress has heard from the lobbyists. It's time to hear from the rest of us.

---

**We're telling Congress: binding rules, not voluntary promises**

This week FRC files our formal comment on Congress's first bipartisan AI bill, the Great American AI Act. Thanks to members who packed our Hill meetings in September — you moved this.

The draft has real strengths: it would require frontier AI companies to publish safety plans, report serious incidents, submit to independent audits, and protect whistleblowers. But it would also freeze the only binding frontier safety laws in the country — California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois's new law — for three years, while giving labs 15 days to report a stolen model or a system that's slipped out of control. New York and Illinois require 72 hours.

AI's most powerful systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they're safe. Our asks are simple: binding, not voluntary. A floor, not a ceiling. Verify before deploy.

Watch your inbox for how to email your representative this week.
---

Q1 (Majority E&C staff): "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?"

CAISI's standards are voluntary and its budget is about $15 million this year. The audits are semi-annual, paid for by the company being audited, and the whole regime sunsets in three years. That's a floor you can't stand on. Make it binding: 72-hour reporting, mandatory pre-deployment testing authority, funding that matches the job, no sunset — and no preemption while any of that is weaker than what states already enforce. Q2 (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned): "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"
Answer: Dropped — yes, we'd support moving forward, with our strengthening asks (72-hour reporting, mandatory pre-deployment testing, funding, no sunset). Shortened — no. Sec. 121 freezes SB 53, RAISE and Illinois' SB 315 while the draft's own duties are weaker (15-day reporting; a narrower definition of critical safety incident) and expire on the same three-year schedule. A two-year or one-year freeze still means a year of no state response during the fastest capability change anyone has measured. If preemption must stay, make it a real floor: a savings clause for stronger state laws and no preemption where the federal duty is weaker.

Second, the most acute risks are national security risks — cyber, bio, model-weight theft — and verifying them protects the defense and infrastructure ecosystem US leadership rests on. Third, we don't take our safety rules from China: the UK funds its AI safety institute better than we fund ours. Leading scientists, including the heads of our own labs, put extinction risk alongside pandemics and nuclear war. If they're wrong, we've spent money on verification. If they're right, we've bought the future.

# Comment letter — DRAFT for Executive Director sign-off (FRC-POL-2026-062)

**NOTE TO ED:** Not for transmission until signed. Section numbers checked against the sponsors' discussion draft and section-by-section (4 June 2026). Mail to GAAIA@mail.house.gov on release.

---

FRONTIER RESTRAINT COALITION
Washington, DC
[letterhead address / phone / email]

23 October 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 — discussion draft**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft, and for inviting comment. This letter is the Frontier Restraint Coalition's formal response. We are a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers who want binding, enforceable limits on the most powerful AI systems.

AI is already doing real good — helping doctors, teachers and working people — and nothing we ask would slow ordinary AI. Our concern is frontier systems: the small number of models trained at a scale that no one, including the companies building them, can yet verify is safe.

The stakes are not ordinary. In May 2023, hundreds of leading AI scientists and the heads of the major laboratories signed one sentence: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." That warning came from the people best placed to know, and it has never been retracted. This year the risk moved off the whiteboard. Frontier models released with unprecedented offensive cyber capabilities caught the federal government unprepared: the White House stood up a hurried interagency task force, and the agency that defends our critical infrastructure still lacked access to one of the systems weeks after release (Institute for Progress). In June, the Commerce Department improvised — using export controls to cut off foreign access to one of these models, on authorities never designed for frontier AI (Lawfare). In September, Anthropic's own chief executive called for a global slowdown in how fast frontier capabilities advance, because risk prevention needs time to keep up.

The people building these systems are telling you the risk is real. Congress should write rules that match it: binding, not voluntary.

**What we support**

The draft does what earlier federal proposals refused to do — it treats frontier risk as a governance problem, not a press-release problem. We support, and ask you to keep:

- **Sec. 102** — codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) at Commerce, with authority to evaluate frontier systems and monitor AI progress.
- **Sec. 111** — requiring large frontier developers to write, implement, comply with and publicly post a frontier AI framework, plus transparency reports with each new frontier model.
- **Sec. 111(f)–(g)** — critical safety incident reporting to CAISI, civil penalties up to $1 million per day, and a reporting role for state attorneys general who opt in.
- **Sec. 112** — independent verification organization (IVO) audits, with mandated access to unredacted materials, records, personnel and systems, and referral of violations to federal and state enforcers.
- **Sec. 113** — anti-retaliation protection for AI whistleblowers, covering employees and contractors, non-waivable by contract or arbitration.

That is a genuine foundation, and we thank you for it. Our objection is that the draft pairs it with one provision that would leave Americans less protected than they are today, and several gaps that leave the federal standard weaker than the state laws it would displace.

**1. Sec. 121 — delete the preemption of state AI law. A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling.**

Sec. 121 would preempt, for three years, any state or local law "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model. In practice that freezes the only binding frontier rules on the books — California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois' SB 315 — which is why the sponsors' own materials list them as covered. For three years, no state could respond to the harms its residents actually experience. At the pace capabilities are changing, three years is an eternity.

Three points weigh against the provision as drafted:

*The federal floor is weaker than what it would displace.* The draft requires incident reporting within 15 days; New York and Illinois require 72 hours. The draft's definition of "critical safety incident" omits a category both states cover — a model using deceptive techniques to subvert its developer's controls or monitoring — which is precisely the failure mode frontier researchers fear most. And it exempts developers under $50 million in revenue from reporting, a carve-out no state frontier law contains.

*The floor expires at the same moment as the freeze.* We understand Secs. 111 and 112 themselves sunset after three years absent reauthorization. The protections offered in exchange for the freeze lapse on the same schedule, leaving no binding rules at all if Congress does not act.

*The scope is unsettled law.* "Development" is defined broadly — training, fine-tuning, substantial modification, and pre-deployment safety and capability evaluations. Legal commentators across the spectrum expect courts to read the clause functionally, sweeping in state safety laws whose practical effect is on model development. A state attorney general opted in to enforce federal standards is not a substitute for a state legislature free to set stronger ones.

Congress has already ruled on the underlying question. In July 2025, the Senate voted 99 to 1 to strip a broader state-AI freeze from the reconciliation bill. Our August 2026 national survey (n=1,5
... [1756 chars truncated] ...
redacted access. Two weaknesses remain. The developer retains and pays its own verifier — an arrangement that reliably produces the audit the customer wants. And audits run semi-annually and on request, while frontier models ship continuously; a system released in March may not be examined until September.

**Requested changes:** (a) CAISI, not the developer, assigns the IVO, with rotation to prevent capture. (b) Require a pre-deployment audit of each new or substantially modified frontier model, in addition to semi-annual reviews. (c) Require publication of a summary of audit findings and remediation. (d) Delete the three-year sunset on Secs. 111 and 112 — safety obligations should not lapse on a timer.

**4. Add a federal licence for frontier training runs.**

The draft licenses auditors but not the activity being audited. No federal law requires anyone to obtain permission before starting a training run above a threshold the draft itself defines — 10^26 integer or floating-point operations. New York will require large frontier developers to register with the state beginning this November. This summer the administration reached for export controls precisely because it had no purpose-built tool, and it has publicly floated an FDA-style pre-deployment licensing regime. Congress should build that tool deliberately, with due process, rather than leave the executive to improvise.

**Requested change:** Add a licence requirement, administered by Commerce, for training runs above the frontier compute threshold, conditioned on a compliant frontier AI framework, a model-weight security plan, capability evaluations, and incident reporting — with authority to suspend the licence for material violations.

**5. Sec. 102 — CAISI needs testing authority it can use, and money it can spend.**

Codifying CAISI is the right call. But as drafted, CAISI's standards are voluntary, and its evaluation work sits inside a federal posture that remains voluntary: the June executive order set up *voluntary* agency reviews of frontier models. Voluntary commitments have not held. The lesson of this year is that the government's ability to *verify before deploy* cannot depend on a company's willingness to cooperate.

On resources, $100 million a year for FY2027–2029 is an authorization, not a fact on the ground. CAISI received $10 million in FY2026 appropriations and operates on a working budget of roughly $15 million. The Institute for Progress estimates at least $84 million a year is needed just to cover CAISI's existing readiness taskings — before GAAIA adds IVO licensing, audit review and enforcement support. The OSTP Director told Congress that CAISI "can certainly benefit from more resources." Our recommendation is a floor of $250 million a year.

**Requested changes:** (a) Give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority over frontier models, with access that does not depend on consent and due process for affected developers. (b) Authorize funding well above $100 million a year — at least $250 million — with an authorization running beyond FY2029. (c) Fund the IVO regime directly, so it does not depend on fees paid by the companies being audited.

**6. Sec. 113 — whistleblower protections no weaker than California's.**

The draft's protections are strong on paper, including non-waiver of arbitration rights and double back pay. We ask that they at least match SB 53, which gives employees a direct, protected channel to the state attorney general.

**Requested changes:** (a) Expressly protect disclosures to state attorneys general and to CAISI. (b) Protect public disclosure where an employee reasonably believes there is an imminent risk to public safety. (c) Confirm that Sec. 121 does not extinguish SB 53's whistleblower channel for frontier-AI employees.

**One housekeeping note**

We understand the frontier provisions of the discussion draft have since been introduced as the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925, 23 July 2026), which moves to 72-hour incident reporting — a change we welcome. We submit these comments on the discussion draft, which remains the vehicle open for stakeholder comment; they apply with equal force to any successor text.

**Conclusion**

Our members are parents who want their children to grow up, workers who want their jobs to last, and researchers who read the capability charts. We are not asking you to choose between innovation and safety. We are asking you to decline a false choice the rest of us cannot afford. The most powerful systems ever built should carry binding, enforceable requirements: a floor, not a ceiling; verify before deploy; 72 hours, not 15 days; a licence to train, and the funding to check the work. We welcome the chance to work with your staffs, and with the Energy and Commerce Committee, as this text moves toward introduction and markup.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

---

**Selected sources on file with FRC:** sponsors' discussion draft text and section-by-section (4 June 2026); sponsors' press release and FAQ (obernolte.house.gov; trahan.house.gov); Roll Call, Axios and GovTech (4 June 2026); Future of Privacy Forum, "Frontier AI Goes Federal" (9 June 2026); Lawfare, "The Case for (Fixing) the Great American AI Act"; Institute for Progress, "What Will It Cost for the US to Be Ready for the Next Big AI Breakthrough?"; FedScoop (OSTP Director on CAISI resourcing); Politico West Wing Playbook (20 Aug. 2026); Cal. SB 53 (Stats. 2025, ch. 138; effective 1 Jan. 2026); N.Y. RAISE Act chapter amendment (signed 27 Mar. 2026; effective 1 Jan. 2027); Ill. SB 315 (P.A. 104-0538; signed 6 July 2026); Center for AI Safety, Statement on AI Risk (30 May 2023); Exec. order, "Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence," 90 Fed. Reg. 58500 (16 Dec. 2025); White House National Policy Framework for AI — Legislative Recommendations (20 Mar. 2026); FRC national survey, Aug. 2026 (n=1,512 registered voters, MOE ±2.5).
